title: When I feel left out
keyIdea: Being left out can feel sad and lonely, and it is OK to say so. Name the feeling, then try a step that helps: ask to join, find someone else, or start a new game. Hurting back, mean words and hiding the feeling make it worse. If it keeps happening, or someone does it on purpose, tell a grown-up.
familyTip: Ask about playtime: “Who did you play with today? Was anyone on their own?” If your child says “I don’t care” about being left out, gently name it: “It sounds like you felt left out.” Make a three-line plan together, and say which grown-ups at school they can tell. If you hear it is the same children every day, tell the school.

visual.caption: Does this step help, or make it worse? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Find someone else to play with
Tell a grown-up if it keeps happening

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name Mia’s feeling, pick the steps that help, find who is on their own, sort once from keeps happening, then make your own plan.

kid: Your friends play a game. They do not ask you. You feel sad. Your tummy feels heavy. That feeling is called being left out. It is OK to feel it.
Say the feeling to yourself: “I feel left out.” Then pick a step that helps. Ask, “Can I play too?” Find someone else. Or start a new game.
Do not hurt back. Do not knock their game down or shout mean words. That makes it worse. Do not hide it and say “I don’t care.”
Look around. Is someone else on their own? Ask them to play. If the same thing keeps happening, or someone does it on purpose, tell a grown-up. You can always tell a grown-up how you feel.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. The PSHE Association Programme of Study asks key stage 1 children to recognise when they or someone else feels lonely and what to do. The DfE Relationships Education guidance (2019) says friendships have ups and downs and children should know how to seek help when a friendship makes them unhappy. The Health Education guidance adds that isolation and loneliness affect children, and that talking to an adult matters.

The lab follows the order children need in the moment. First name the feeling, which many children hide behind “I don’t care”. Then choose a step that helps: ask to join, find another child or start a new game. Then look around, because another child is often on their own too. Last, tell the difference between a one-off (the game was full) and a pattern (the same child says “Nobody play with Mia” every day).

Common mistakes: thinking “I don’t care” means a child is fine; believing that hurting back or shouting will get them into the game; standing and staring until the group gives in; deciding a friend who plays with someone new is no longer a friend; and keeping repeated, deliberate exclusion secret. The Anti-Bullying Alliance counts leaving someone out on purpose, again and again, as a form of bullying, so that is the moment for a grown-up. Be careful not to suggest children must sort everything out alone: telling a grown-up how they feel is always allowed.

This lesson is about the feeling and what to do next. The lesson Asking to join in covers how to watch a game and ask well. In the lab your child names Mia’s feeling, picks the steps that help, finds the two children who are alone, sorts once from keeps happening, and makes a three-line plan.

practice.prompt: Your friends start a game and do not ask you. Your tummy feels heavy. What is this feeling called?
practice.hint: Proud and excited are happy feelings. Which one is sad?
practice.explain: Feeling left out. It is a real feeling, and naming it is the first step.

practice.prompt: There are {n} children on the bench, each one on their own. Mia asks them all to play. How many children are playing with Mia?
practice.hint: Mia asked every child on the bench.
practice.explain: All {n} of them. When you feel left out, someone else may be on their own too.

practice.prompt: Mia feels left out of a tower game. What step helps?
practice.hint: Which step does not hurt anyone?
practice.explain: Asking helps. Knocking the tower down or shouting makes it worse.

practice.prompt: There are 5 school days in a week. Jo left Mia out on {n} of them. On how many days did Jo not leave her out?
practice.hint: Count the days Jo left Mia out, then take {n} away from 5.
practice.explain: 5 take away {n} is {=5-n}. If it keeps happening day after day, Mia should tell a grown-up.

practice.prompt: Every day, Jo says “Nobody play with Mia.” What should Mia do?
practice.hint: It keeps happening, and Jo does it on purpose.
practice.explain: Tell a grown-up. When it keeps happening or is on purpose, a grown-up can help.

pool.prompt: Leo says, “I don’t care that they didn’t ask me.” His head is down. What might be true?
choices: He may be hiding a sad feeling
pool.hint: Look at his head. Does it match his words?
pool.explain: He may be hiding a sad feeling. Saying “I feel left out” is braver than hiding it.

pool.prompt: The game is full today. What can Ava do?
choices: Find someone else to play with
Stand and stare until they let her in
pool.hint: If one game is full, is there another way to play?
pool.explain: Find someone else, or start a new game. Staring or grabbing does not help.

pool.prompt: Ben’s friend played with a new child today. What is true?
choices: Friends can play with other people too
Ben should be mean to the new child
pool.hint: Can you have more than one friend?
pool.explain: Friends can play with others too. It does not mean the friendship is over.

pool.prompt: Kids laugh and run off each time Sam comes over. This happens every day. What should Sam do?
pool.hint: Is this once, or does it keep happening?
pool.explain: Tell a grown-up. It keeps happening and it is on purpose, so Sam needs help.

pool.prompt: Mia tried {n} steps that help. Then she tried {k} more. How many helpful steps did she try?
pool.hint: Start at {n} and count on {k} more steps.
pool.explain: {n} and {k} make {=n+k}. If one step does not work, try another.

pool.prompt: Is it OK to feel sad when you are left out?
choices: Yes, it is a real feeling
No, you must pretend you don’t mind
pool.hint: Do grown-ups feel left out sometimes too?
pool.explain: Yes. Everyone can feel left out sometimes. It is OK to feel it and to say it.

pool.prompt: Lily is on her own by the tree. You feel left out too. What could you do?
choices: Ask Lily, “Do you want to play?”
pool.hint: Could Lily feel left out too?
pool.explain: Ask Lily to play. It can help you both feel better.

pool.prompt: Which step makes being left out worse?
pool.hint: Which one hurts the other children?
pool.explain: Knocking their game down. Hurting back gets you into trouble and does not get you into the game.

pool.prompt: The game was full once, today. Can Mia still tell a grown-up how she feels?
choices: Yes, you can always tell a grown-up
No, only if someone hits her
No, grown-ups do not want to know
pool.hint: Is talking about your feelings ever wrong?
pool.explain: Yes. You can always tell a grown-up how you feel, even if it only happened once.

pool.prompt: {n} children were left out at playtime. Mia asked {k} of them to play. How many are still on their own?
pool.hint: Start with {n} children, then take away the {k} Mia asked.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}. Looking around for someone on their own helps them and you.
